articles.title_zh: Hayden Panettiere Died From Toxic Effects of Fentanyl, Other Drugs
articles.content_orig:
Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose involving fentanyl, coroner says
The investigation into the 36-year-old US actress’ death is ongoing, police say
US actress Hayden Panettiere died from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, a coroner in South Carolina said on Tuesday.
Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home.
According to a statement from the Greenville County Coroner’s Office, a combination of fentanyl and its chemical by-product, as well as the anti-anxiety medication alprazolam, a muscle relaxant and a drug used to treat major depression and other serious mental health disorders, was found in Panettiere’s system.
The office did not include further details from the autopsy report in its initial release.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures inch higher after Nasdaq Composite posts fresh record: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures inch higher after Nasdaq Composite posts fresh record: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026.
U.S. equity futures were trading marginally higher early Wednesday as oil prices and bond yields eased on hopes for potential de-escalation in the war between the U.S. and Iran.
In Tuesday's regular trading, the Dow fell 0.4%, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.5%, marking its fourth positive session in a row. The tech-heavy index hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record. The S&P 500 finished marginally lower, but remains about 0.7% off from its all-time high.
In Asia-Pacific, South Korea's Kospi rose 0.9%, while Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 inched higher. Mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.6% lower. Japan's markets were closed for a holiday.
Brett Ewing, chief market strategist at First Franklin Financial Services, told CNBC he thought the S&P 500 could hit 8,200 before the year is through.
"Our call at the beginning of the year was 8,000 on the S&P. We raised our target, believe it or not, in August to 8,200 by year-end," he said.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours during the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
Oil prices eased slightly, with both Brent crude oil and West Texas Intermediate slipping roughly 1% each in the session.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that the U.S. is deciding whether to prohibit exports of diesel, which reached a national average price of $6.53 per gallon, according to AAA.
"We're examining whether it's feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work," Bessent said during a bilateral meeting between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the United Nations.
Going into Wednesday, traders will be watching earnings results from General Mills, Paychex and H.B. Fuller.
Brent crude oil futures turn positive
International benchmark Brent crude futures for November delivery were last seen trading almost 0.6% higher at $99.74 a barrel, reversing early losses. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November remained in negative territory, falling 0.3% to $90.19 per barrel.
Fed’s Collins warns inflation could stay ‘notably’ higher than 2% target
Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins has warned that there is "an increased likelihood" that inflation will stay "notably" above the Federal Reserve's 2% target.
Explaining her reasoning for backing the Fed's quarter-point interest rate hike last week, Collins wrote in a LinkedIn post that a "somewhat more restrictive federal funds rate will help ensure that inflation durably returns to target."
Bitcoin was trading around $86,251.47 early Wednesday morning, after rising as high as $86,349.90 the previous day — its highest level since late January.
It marked a 0.2% intraday decline.
Ether was also down 0.2% Wednesday, trading at just over $2,748.
Ripple bucked the trend, adding 1.7% to trade at $1.61.
European stocks extend gains
European shares opened in positive territory on Wednesday, building on a winning session the previous day that saw the regional Stoxx 600 rise more than 1%.
At 8:20 a.m. in London (3:20 a.m. ET), the pan-European index was up by 0.2%.
Tech and banking stocks led gains in the region, while utilities stocks — which often rise during periods of risk-off sentiment — led losses in early trading.
South Korea's Kospi gains 0.9%, China's CSI 300 falls 0.6%
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.90% to 7,080.92, while Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 inched higher to 8,765.30.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was down 1.01% in the last hour of trade on Wednesday, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.60% lower at 4,517.28.
Japan's markets were closed for a holiday.
Treasury yields edge lower
Yields on U.S. Treasurys fell across the curve early Wednesday, as oil prices extended their decline.
As of 3 a.m. ET, the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury was 2 basis points lower at 4.947%. The 2-year Treasury yield fell 2 basis points to 4.758%, while the 30-year Treasury yield was 2 basis points lower at 5.287%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Yields moved lower in tandem with oil prices, which were on track for their sixth consecutive day of losses on Wednesday.
Oil prices set for longest downturn in over a year
Brent crude oil futures fell early Wednesday, extending losses to trade at $98.57 per barrel.
It marked a sixth straight day of declines, putting front-month contracts on track for their longest losing streak since August 2025.
South Korean solar stocks jump as curbs on Chinese sector expected to remain in place
Shares of South Korean solar companies Hanwha Solutions and OCI Holdings jumped more than 8% on Wednesday, as U.S. restrictions on Chinese solar products came into focus ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
The two leaders are set to meet in Washington this week, with trade expected to be among the key issues discussed.
Hana Securities said it was highly unlikely that the U.S. would ease restrictions on Chinese solar products as part of the talks, arguing that Washington increasingly views solar as a strategic industry tied to national security.
"If the U.S. were to ease restrictions on Chinese solar products at the U.S.-China summit, it would effectively mean stepping back from efforts to build a domestic supply chain for a strategic national security asset," analyst Yoon Jae-sung said in a note Wednesday.
Oil falls after U.S. and Iran talk for hours at UN meeting
Oil fell Wednesday, amid optimism that supply disruptions would ease following U.S.-Iran talks which raised hopes of a diplomatic solution to the conflict in the Middle East.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for November delivery dropped 0.75% at $98.51 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November fell 1.03% at $89.59 per barrel.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. officials had a "very good meeting" with Iran's delegation and that it lasted about three hours. Earlier in his address to the U.N., Trump said he had a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
Mainland China and Hong Kong shares open lower
Mainland China stocks and Hong Kong shares opened lower, with investors continuing to keep watch for developments relating to Chinese leader Xi Jinping's state visit to the U.S. this week.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped 0.68%, while mainland China's CSI 300 was 0.13% lower.
The losses in Hang Seng were led by financials and industrials sectors, down 0.35% and 0.16%, respectively.
Asia-Pacific markets open higher amid hopes of diplomatic solution to Mideast conflict
Asia-Pacific markets traded higher early Wednesday, amid lower oil prices following U.S.-Iran talks which raised hopes of a diplomatic solution to the Mideast conflict.
The Kospi added 1.79% at open, while the small-cap Kosdaq gained 0..84%.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was 0.34% higher.
Japan's markets are closed for a holiday.
Asia-Pacific markets set to open higher following talks between the U.S. and Iran
Asia-Pacific markets were set to open higher Wednesday, as signs of easing tensions in the Middle East helped to buoy investor sentiment following Iran-U.S. talks.
Hong Kong Hang Seng index futures were at 25,133, compared with the index's last close of 25,087.75.
Futures for Australia's S&P/ASX 200 last traded at 8,822, while the index closed at 8,757.80.
Japan's markets are closed for a holiday.
President Donald Trump said that U.S. officials had a "very good meeting" with Iran's delegation and that it lasted about three hours. That raised hopes that a diplomatic solution to the Mideast conflict may be on the horizon.

articles.title_orig: Category 5 Hurricane Polo is 'one of the strongest storms ever'
articles.title_zh: Category 5 Hurricane Polo is 'one of the strongest storms ever'
articles.content_orig:
Category 5 Hurricane Polo is 'one of the strongest storms ever'
MEXICO CITY — Hurricane Polo has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades, and it was expected to skirt Mexico's southwestern coast as a Category 5 storm.
Polo was an "extremely dangerous" storm with maximum sustained winds of 165 mph (265 kph), the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said Tuesday night.
Polo was centered 210 miles (338 kilometers) south of Zihuatanejo, Mexico, and nearly stationary over the Pacific Ocean. The hurricane center said Polo was expected to start a slow but sharp turn northwest during the night and then travel in a generally west-northwestward direction over the next several days.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts indicated that the hurricane was not likely to touch land. Still, the NHC said hurricane-force winds are happening up to 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the storm's center and tropical storm-force winds up to 105 miles (169 kilometers) away.
The hurricane set residents along Mexico's Pacific coast on edge once again after being walloped by powerful cyclones a number of times in recent years. Beaches emptied out and dark clouds swirled above choppy seas, while Mexican authorities temporarily suspended classes Tuesday in a number of areas. Mexico's navy shut down ports in the states of Guerrero and Michoacán and warned civilians and fishermen to take care.
Waves, flooding and mudslides are all risks
Concepción López Villegas was busily preparing her seaside restaurant for what may come. Strong waves were already lapping at the coastline of her city Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán. As men and children watched the stirring waters behind her, López Villegas said she feared powerful waves would destroy the small business she has worked decades to build.
"We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed."
National Hurricane Center data shows that Polo has reached speeds comparable to only a few hurricanes to form in the region in recent decades, primarily Hurricane Patricia, which reached 215 mph (346 kph) in 2015.
"This is one of the strongest storms ever in the (Pacific) Basin," said Kristen L. Corbosiero, professor at the University at Albany's Department of Atmospheric & Environmental Sciences.
The NHC warned that tropical storm conditions were expected along the Pacific coast in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima states.
Heavy rain could produce flash flooding and mudslides. About 3 to 6 inches (8 to 15 centimeters) of rain was forecast for Guerrero and Michoacán states, with smaller amounts possible for coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states.
El Niño fueled rapid intensification
The U.S. Embassy in Mexico issued a weather alert, instructing citizens to avoid water and beaches and to heed warnings from Mexican authorities.
"Even if the storm does not make direct landfall, heavy rain may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Hazardous ocean conditions—intensified by storms—may result in deadly rip currents and rogue waves," the embassy wrote in a statement.
The rapid intensification of the storm has stunned scientists and authorities alike, with the NHC writing in a report that it was "truly remarkable" how quickly Polo gained strength in the past 24 hours.
Philip Klotzbach, research scientist in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University, attributed the intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region.
In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said.
"There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said.
Polo is the third Category 5 hurricane of the Pacific season, following Genevieve and Lowell earlier this year. Category 5 is the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale, reflecting that a storm has maximum sustained winds exceeding 157 mph (253 kph).
No Atlantic hurricanes have formed yet this year, and this year has set a record for the longest start to a season without a hurricane. The effects of this year's El Niño crush storms before they get going.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
articles.title_zh: Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
articles.content_orig:
Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials said Tuesday they plan to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging that the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program, or simply do not exist.
Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
"We're actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them," said Vance, who leads a government task force to eliminate fraud. He was flanked by Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, and other administration officials.
Vance said the cancellation of approximately 315,000 enrollments covering 760,000 people was done in part because the government was not checking whether people enrolled were eligible. Vance said another 419,000 enrollments will get additional verification to make sure they are eligible for the benefit.
The Trump administration also announced a six-month suspension on new agents or brokers who sign up enrollees for healthcare coverage, who officials say commit a disproportionate amount of the fraud they uncovered.
Roughly 19.2 million Americans are actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans as of early 2026, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by former President Joe Biden.
Tuesday's announcement is the latest in an initiative by the Trump administration to address fraud around the country, including in federal healthcare programs, which officials say is needed to rein in runaway spending and protect taxpayers.
Some healthcare policy experts are calling for more transparency on how the Trump administration decided to cut hundreds of thousands of enrollees — and question how many people may have been wrongly cut from the program.
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said "I think there's no question that somebody who was fraudulently enrolled should have their coverage canceled," however, "I think the question is whether this was the appropriate process by which to identify fraudulent enrollees, and also whether all of them were indeed fraudulently enrolled."
Cox said the elimination of the people from ACA programs was done outside of the normal regulatory process.
Ellen Montz, a former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at CMS during the Biden administration said during her time in government, there was an ongoing effort to eliminate fraud from ACA programs.
"There's a lot of work to be done, and the Trump administration has done some good things that are targeting the actual fraudsters," she said. Adding that Tuesday's announcement lacked details on how the administration determined who to cut. " I would imagine we'll hear from some subset of consumers that ask: why did my enrollment get cancelled?" Montz said.
At the press conference, Tuesday, Vance referred to some enrollments lacking social security numbers or immigration documentation.
The announcement comes as stubbornly high inflation and rising healthcare costs pressure the Trump administration to come up with a plan to bring down costs for Americans as affordability remains a central issue in the fall midterm elections.
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many Americans during Trump's second term, after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Biden's term.
Premiums doubled or tripled for many enrollees, prompting millions to downgrade their plans or exit the program entirely after the Republican-led Congress allowed the subsidies to expire this year.
The Government Accountability Office suggests fraud risks in the advance premium tax credit do exist - however it's unclear at what scale. The GAO conducted covert testing using fictitious ACA applicants enrolled in 2024 and 2025. A report released in December showed that the federal marketplace approved subsidized coverage for almost all of the GAO's 24 fake enrollees.
The White House referred The Associated Press to the Vice President's team for additional comment on bigger plans to address healthcare affordability. The Vice President's office and CMS did not respond to Associated Press requests for comment.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news of the Trump administration's plan to remove ACA enrollees from public exchanges.
Democratic lawmakers criticized the move to remove enrollees from ACA coverage.
Richard E. Neal, a Massachusetts Democrat and ranking member of the Ways and Means Committee, said "Republicans have already created the worst healthcare crisis ever, but every decision by the Trump Administration is designed to keep making it worse."
"As if making coverage harder to access through skyrocketing premiums and more red tape wasn't painful enough, they're doubling down to take it away entirely," Neal said.

articles.title_orig: White House Defends Trump’s Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico in Court Filing
articles.title_zh: White House Defends Trump’s Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico in Court Filing
articles.content_orig:
The Justice Department said late Tuesday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico can be shut out from areas of the White House at the president’s will. The lawyers argue that the outlets’ coverage of the Iran war and of President Donald Tump’s ballroom construction could amount to a national security risk that justifies the ban.
A court filing from the Trump administration late Tuesday night argues “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” in spite of First Amendment protections around press freedom.
The filing also argues Trump can control private areas of the White House to protect national security information that may be inside the complex – an argument in line with other abrupt lockdowns and changes Trump has made to the White House.
“At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote to the court.
“The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns.”
The filings came on the eve of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. CNN, MS NOW and Politico are asking for the court to immediately restore their access to the White House.
The case is a critical test of First Amendment protections and has prompted suspensions of live coverage of Trump by the major TV networks, National Public Radio and still photographers in the White House press corps.
While the Justice Department is arguing for the president’s prerogatives, the federal court in Washington, DC, has repeatedly restored journalists’ press access at the White House when administrations have tried to take it away. That includes by setting the law in the nation’s capital in favor of press freedoms and due process protections for news outlets.
New letters to outlets citing stories about East Wing ballroom, Iran war
The new court filings include letters to the three outlets, dated Tuesday, explaining the president’s cited reasons for the ban. A key claim the media companies have made in the case is that the White House violated their due process rights by failing to give them any written warning before cutting off their access and by depriving the journalists the opportunity to contest the ban. The DOJ pointed to the letters to argue that the due process claims should fail.
The letters cite various stories published by the news organizations and give the reporters until Friday to offer written submissions objecting to the bans.
The letter to CNN cites its reporting on Trump’s plans to build a “top secret” bunker below the East Wing ballroom he is constructing, as well as several stories by the network about the Iran war.
It said CNN had failed to uphold the “expectations” of White House press badge holders because of “reporting incidents” that “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods.”
The letter to MS NOW, meanwhile, criticizes its coverage of the war in Iran and a story about a leak probe, while Politico was targeted because of stories related to the Iran, the ballroom and Russia sanctions discussions.
This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.content_orig:
Austin ICE shooting proves we've lost ability to wait for facts | Opinion
Democrats are right to demand answers about the Austin shooting. They're wrong to treat ICE itself as illegitimate.
The shooting of a man in Austin by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has become the latest flashpoint in America's divide over enforcing immigration law.
Protests erupted in Texas' capital city on Sept. 20 after an ICE agent shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, a Venezuelan DoorDash driver.
CNN reported that bystander video shows an ICE agent’s vehicle striking Garcés Pérez’s car, followed by gunshots. At a Sept. 21 news conference, calling in from detention, Garcés Pérez denied running from the agent, disputing the Department of Homeland Security’s account of a foot pursuit.
According to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez was released from the hospital straight into ICE custody, with no pain medication. She told reporters he entered the United States in 2024 through the Biden-era CBP One app, had a work permit and was seeking asylum, but received a deportation order in absentia after a hearing notice was sent to the wrong address.
Garcés Pérez should not be deported until the investigation is complete.
DHS revoked CBP One parolees' status when President Donald Trump returned to office, though a federal judge has since ordered it restored pending litigation.
In a lengthy statement released on Sept. 22, DHS refuted claims that Garcés Pérez was not receiving proper medical care, stated that his work permit expired in 2025, and reminded the public that resisting arrest and evading officers is dangerous for all involved.
The Austin American-Statesman reported that video footage calls into question Garcés Pérez's claim that he didn't flee agents.
DHS posted on X that it is investigating with the FBI, maintaining that Garcés Pérez "illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal."
CBS News reported that the ICE officer who shot him has been placed on administrative leave.
Austin's Democratic leaders reacted with fury. Mayor Kirk Watson said he wants the city's police department to participate in the investigation as a third party. U.S. Rep. Greg Casar went further.
"The vast majority of people being pulled over have zero criminal records," Casar told reporters Sept. 21. "ICE has not made us more safe by arresting 5-year-olds, by shooting delivery drivers, by raiding construction sites. We will all be more safe when ICE gets the hell out of Austin, Texas."
Democrats continue to oppose enforcing immigration law
I support ICE, and incidents like this still frustrate me. The use of force here is troubling, and there are two competing accounts of what happened and Garcés Pérez's legal status.
Texans deserve the truth. Democrats are right to demand answers about the Austin shooting. They're wrong to treat ICE itself as illegitimate. Local officials should be pushing federal agents to enforce the law well, not undermining the agency tasked with our security.
On Sept. 22, the ranking members of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform held a hearing on the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. Good and Pretti were U.S. citizens who interfered with ICE operations.
The congressional hearing also reviewed other deaths, including Ruben Ray Martinez and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine.
ICE’s critics have legitimate concerns. These cases deserve answers, and ICE agents should be held accountable while DHS works to prevent unnecessary casualties. But even with all the questions I have about the Austin shooting, it's frustrating to watch Texas Democrats immediately condemn ICE wholesale, telling the agency in no uncertain terms to "get the hell out."
In January, Casar urged Senate Democrats to reject ICE funding, part of a broader pattern of Democrats calling to defund or abolish the agency after incidents like this one. Treating ICE as illegitimate is irresponsible. Enforcing immigration law is a legitimate function of government – one of its most important.
ICE is necessary to maintain law and order
A city or state that won't enforce the law isn't safe for its citizens. A country without secure borders is ripe for crisis and chaos. I'm glad Trump is reining this in through ICE, even though there have been mistakes.
Successful efforts rarely make news, even as they make communities safer. ICE said a recent five-day Indiana operation led to 426 arrests of people here illegally, including some with criminal histories involving sex crimes and assault. Its Dallas field office announced 39 people indicted or charged after a child exploitation operation. And in July, ICE made nearly 50,000 arrests, the highest monthly total of Trump's second term.
Democratic lawmakers rarely applaud these successes, and they show little of the same sympathy for the victims of illegal immigration.
They're right to demand answers about the Austin shooting. But they're wrong to call for ICE to leave Texas. Secure borders and safe cities depend on it staying.
Nicole Russell is an opinion columnist with USA TODAY. She lives in Texas with her four kids. Sign up for her newsletter, The Right Track, and get it delivered to your inbox.

新视频揭示了奥斯汀ICE枪击案发生前的追捕行动，但关键时刻仍未被发现
得克萨斯州奥斯汀——新视频揭示了周日北奥斯汀ICE枪击案的筹备情况，尽管关键时刻仍然缺失。
奥斯汀警方发布了一段视频，显示ICE特工在枪击事件发生前与威尔伯·加西斯·佩雷斯的蓝色汽车在一起，以及随后执法部门的反应。然而，该视频不包括枪声或从最初停止到拍摄之间的10-15分钟。
相关| ICE参与北奥斯汀枪击案后，居民聚集在一起纪念
一名下班的奥斯汀警探恰好在附近，在进入附近的一家购物中心之前，用Garcés Pérez的个人行车记录仪在他的车辆附近抓获了ICE特工。据奥斯汀警察局官员称，在接下来的10到15分钟内，有一辆车在附近的街区被追赶，但该部门澄清说，没有证据表明有人徒步追赶。
奥斯汀警察局长丽莎·戴维斯说：“我们有一些视频，我们正在处理一段经过那里一些街区的追捕视频，并在那里结束。”。
警方表示，这段时间的视频是存在的，调查人员仍在努力收集和处理。目前尚不清楚的是，加西亚·佩雷斯为什么离开最初的交通站，沿途发生了什么事件，以及导致立交桥下发生枪击事件的原因。
Garcés Pérez的律师表示，她的客户报告称被一辆黑色SUV追赶，最初没有意识到这辆车属于执法部门。她说他正试图到达一个更安全的地方，而不是试图逃跑。
APD发布了关于北奥斯汀ICE枪杀委内瑞拉男子的视频
当休班的侦探回到车上时，他开始用手机录音，听到了三声枪响。现场第一名奥斯汀警察的随身摄像机镜头显示了枪击事件后的反应，但发布的视频中没有一段包括枪击发生的时刻。
加西斯·佩雷斯的移民律师凯特·林肯·戈德芬奇说：“我要求ICE提供行车记录仪录像，我不明白他们为什么不把它交给我们。”。
戴维斯警长表示，奥斯汀警方不知道被解雇的ICE特工是否佩戴了随身摄像头。截至周二的新闻发布会，该部门尚未要求联邦当局提供随身摄像头视频或类似材料。

articles.title_orig: Should You Buy Micron Before Sept. 30? 1 Number Could Send the Stock Soaring
articles.title_zh: Should You Buy Micron Before Sept. 30? 1 Number Could Send the Stock Soaring
articles.content_orig:
Micron (MU +5.00%) is set to report fourth-quarter earnings after the bell on Sept. 30.
The memory chip giant has been one of the most closely watched stocks in the AI boom after soaring more than 1,000% as AI compute demand has sparked an unprecedented shortage of memory. As a result, revenue and profits for Micron and its peers have skyrocketed.
As one of the three leading memory chip companies in the world, along with Samsung and SK Hynix, Micron, the only U.S. stock in the group, has emerged as a popular choice for investors who want exposure to the bottleneck.
The stock is likely to swing big following its earnings report, as its results have been difficult for Wall Street to predict, and because the stock is historically volatile due to the cyclicality of memory.
Image source: Getty Images.
The 1 number to watch when Micron reports Q4 earnings
Investors will be tracking key numbers from the quarterly report, like revenue, adjusted earnings per share, and gross margin, and Micron's guidance will help determine where the stock goes next.
However, I think the most important factor in the report will be commentary on market dynamics, particularly for 2028. Yes, 2028, not the company's financial figures, will be the most important number to watch.
2028 is key because the company has already said that its high-bandwidth memory, specifically HBM3E and HBM4, are fully booked through calendar 2027. That means the company's results through the next calendar year are more or less predictable. What's still unknown is how supply and demand dynamics impact the company's performance in 2028 and beyond.
On the Q3 call in June, management said that HBM demand had begun to stretch into 2028, and it also expects new capacity to come online, meaning 2028 could be another bumper year if memory prices remain elevated.
The future outweighs the present for Micron
Where Micron stock goes from here largely depends on investor perception of how long the AI-driven boom will last. That's what's unknown about the stock. Investors are already well aware that the company will make huge profits in fiscal 2027 and 2028, but the cycle will eventually peak. What matters is whether that's five years away or more, or whether it's just two or three years away.
Management commentary on 2028 will give investors the biggest hint about whether the peak of the cycle is getting pushed further out. If we hear a positive update on 2028 or more commentary on tight market dynamics, I think that will push the stock higher. Without that, a gain is less likely.
Micron is insulating itself from the cyclical downside
Micron has already taken steps to protect itself from the other side of the cycle. It has begun signing strategic customer agreements (SCA), most of which last five years. These agreements lock in a price range and are structured as take-or-pay agreements with minimum purchase commitments, protecting Micron from a potential bust in the cycle. The agreements it signed through the third quarter covered about 20% of DRAM volume and 33% of NAND volume, indicating it's protecting a significant share of its business.
While Micron is taking prudent steps with the current memory windfall, it remains bullish on long-term demand, pouring $100 billion into a new manufacturing facility in upstate New York, which is expected to begin producing chips in 2029 or 2030.
Overall, Micron is on solid footing heading into the report. The stock looks cheap relative to near-term earnings forecasts, and it has risen in recent days from a potential surge in CPU demand, driven by Meta Platforms' breakthrough launch of its Muse AI personal agent.
Given those factors, I think the stock is a buy heading into the report, but its commentary about 2028 could be the biggest determinant in where Micron stock goes after the earnings report and over the coming months.

articles.title_orig: Discord’s age verification era is upon us, despite community backlash
articles.title_zh: Discord’s age verification era is upon us, despite community backlash
articles.content_orig:
Starting Wednesday, Discord, the community messaging platform, will roll out age verification measures to all users.
The rollout comes after the company initially delayed its age verification plans in February due to backlash from users concerned that biometric scans and ID checks could jeopardize their privacy. Those concerns weren’t unfounded; last year, a third-party vendor that works with Discord was breached, potentially exposing the data of 70,000 users’ data, including government ID photos and selfies used for identity verification.
“Age assurance draws strong opinions and skepticism, especially when it involves sharing biometric information or a form of ID,” Discord CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy wrote in a blog post, published Tuesday. “At the same time, age assurance laws are expanding, and since my last post we’ve had to launch age assurance in other regions, including in Brazil and in Texas.”
However, Vishnevskiy says more than 90% of Discord users won’t have to verify their age. He explains that Discord will instead use existing account data to detect “signals,” like account tenure (how long an account has existed), device and activity data, and other usage patterns, to determine whether a user belongs in the adult, teen, or unconfirmed age group.
Discord says that it doesn’t estimate users’ ages based on message content, profile data, or demographic attributes.
“The way a typical 15-year-old uses Discord (including how many communities they’re a part of and how they interact with others) looks different in aggregate from how a typical 30-year-old uses Discord,” the company wrote in a separate, technical blog post, also published Tuesday. “Our [machine learning] model has learned these patterns to predict whether a given account likely belongs to an adult or a teen.”
This doesn’t mean that Discord is collecting new user data. It’s standard for social media companies to retain this kind of data on their customers, even though it might feel unsettling to see it spelled out so overtly.
Because local laws have required Discord to use age assurance technology in certain regions due to local law, the company was able to train its model on reliably confirmed data linking user behavior to age.
If Discord is not confident that a user is an adult, that user can still prove their age without a biometric or ID scan. They can appeal by sharing a credit card or age group data from their Apple App Store or Google Play Store account.
For confirmed adults, nothing about the platform will change. Teens accounts, however, will automatically be blocked from accessing age-restricted servers or channels. Message requests from people who aren’t their friends will go to a separate message requests inbox, and teens will get alerts when accepting friend requests from someone they don’t share mutual friends with.
As governments around the world continue passing age verification requirements in an attempt to protect children online, experts warn that these age checks can create a host of new privacy and security issues. That leaves platforms like Discord with a difficult choice: comply or risk sanctions.

articles.title_orig: New Mac Mini Has Two Storage Downsides, Including Unremovable SSD
articles.title_zh: New Mac Mini Has Two Storage Downsides, Including Unremovable SSD
articles.content_orig:
As confirmed by the website "Expand Mac mini," NAND storage in the new Mac mini models with the M6 and M5 Pro chips is soldered to the logic board, whereas the previous models with the M4 and M4 Pro chips have removable storage that can be upgraded.
In other words, the new Mac mini does not support aftermarket storage upgrades.
"Expand Mac mini" offers plug-and-play SSD modules that are functionally equivalent to Apple's proprietary modules, yet hundreds of dollars cheaper. As a result, customers were able to save a significant amount of money by configuring their Mac mini with the minimum 256GB capacity that was available on Apple's online store and later installing a higher-capacity aftermarket module. With the new models, that is no longer possible.
"We will keep looking for an opening, but support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely," the "Expand Mac mini" website said, in a blog post.
Mac mini models with the M1 chip and M2/M2 Pro chips also had NAND soldered to the logic board, so the M4/M4 Pro configurations having removable storage has proven to be a one-off exception for now. Apple has not commented on the reversal.
In addition, all new Mac mini configurations with 256GB of storage reportedly have a single NAND chip, rather than a pair of 128GB chips. As a result, 256GB configurations have slower SSD speeds compared to configurations with 512GB of storage or more that do have dual NAND chips, according to AAPL Ch.'s testing with Blackmagic's Disk Speed Test benchmark tool.
The new 256GB model's Disk Speed Test scores were roughly half that of models with 512GB of storage or more. The average customer is unlikely to notice the difference, but power users will appreciate knowing that they need to opt for at least 512GB of storage in order to achieve the fastest SSD speeds possible.
Fortunately, even with 256GB of storage, it appears that the new Mac mini has meaningfully faster SSD speeds compared to the previous 256GB model.
Mac mini models with M2/M2 Pro and 256GB of storage also had a single NAND chip, so the M4/M4 Pro configurations proved to be a one-off exception for this too.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he backs diesel export ban to curb soaring energy costs
articles.title_zh: 特朗普表示，他支持柴油出口禁令，以遏制能源成本飙升
articles.summary_zh: 唐纳德·特朗普周二表示，他支持禁止柴油出口的想法，一些美国政客呼吁这是遏制能源成本飙升的一种方式。
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump on Tuesday said he backed the idea of a ban on diesel exports, which some US politicians are calling for as a way to curb the soaring cost of energy.
Diesel prices have rallied in Europe and the US to record highs as wars in Iran and Ukraine sharply cut exports from some of the biggest producers such as Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. A gallon of diesel fuel in the US was $6.53 on Tuesday, the highest average on record and over 75% higher than a year ago.
“I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. I’ve called for it within my people,” Trump told reporters ahead of a meeting with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, speaking at the same meeting, said: “We’re examining whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.”
On Sunday, Trump urged Zelenskyy to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices, the Financial Times reported. On social media, Trump wrote that Russia “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry”.
Some Republican Senate candidates in the most competitive midterm races called for the administration to implement the export ban to try to alleviate high costs for Americans.
“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” wrote the US representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican who is in a competitive Senate race in Iowa, on X. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”
In a statement, the American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers trade group said that an export ban would “backfire”, noting that domestic refiners would have to reduce production and “producing less diesel also means producing less gasoline”.
Trump said he and Zelenskiy would discuss Ukrainian attacks on refining sites in Russia.
“It is a serious hit on the Russians. It’s also a serious hit on the price of diesel,” said Trump, who also told reporters the two leaders would discuss working out a solution to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“I think it’s going to happen,” Trump said, of a potential solution to the war.
Reuters contributed reporting
articles.content_zh:
唐纳德·特朗普周二表示，他支持禁止柴油出口的想法，一些美国政客呼吁这是遏制能源成本飙升的一种方式。
欧洲和美国的柴油价格上涨至历史新高，因为伊朗和乌克兰的战争大幅削减了俄罗斯、沙特阿拉伯和阿拉伯联合酋长国等一些最大生产国的出口。周二，美国一加仑柴油的价格为6.53美元，创历史新高，比一年前上涨了75%以上。
特朗普在与乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基会晤前告诉记者：“我说过，我们不要发送柴油。我们生产了很多柴油……我呼吁这样做。我在我的人民中呼吁这样做”。
美国财政部长Scott Bessent在同一次会议上表示：“我们正在研究从整体炼油能力来看是否可行，以及全面或部分禁令是否可行。”
据英国《金融时报》报道，周日，特朗普敦促泽连斯基暂停对俄罗斯炼油厂的罢工，因为担心炼油厂可能会进一步推高油价。特朗普在社交媒体上写道，俄罗斯“不幸失去了对柴油工业的控制”。
在竞争最激烈的中期选举中，一些共和党参议院候选人呼吁政府实施出口禁令，以减轻美国人的高昂成本。
“爱荷华州人正在受到挤压，不应该在加油站或伊朗战争的结账线上买单，”美国众议员阿什利·欣森在X上写道。“我们需要利用我们掌握的每一种选择来缓解高昂的价格。”欣森是一名共和党人，正在爱荷华州参加竞争激烈的参议院竞选
美国燃料和石化制造商贸易组织在一份声明中表示，出口禁令将“适得其反”，并指出国内炼油厂将不得不减产，“减少柴油产量也意味着减少汽油产量”。
特朗普表示，他和泽连斯基将讨论乌克兰对俄罗斯炼油厂的袭击。
特朗普表示：“这对俄罗斯人来说是一个严重打击。这也对柴油价格造成了严重打击。”他还告诉记者，两位领导人将讨论制定一个解决方案来结束俄罗斯在乌克兰的战争。
“我认为这将会发生，”特朗普在谈到战争的潜在解决方案时说。

articles.title_orig: Report: Jaxson Dart’s injury could be season-ending
articles.title_zh: Report: Jaxson Dart’s injury could be season-ending
articles.content_orig:
One day after an apparently serious injury to Bears starting quarterback Caleb Williams ended up being not nearly as bad as it seemed, an injury to Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart has turned out to be far worse than believed.
Via NFL Network, an MRI showed that Dart’s knee injury is worse than expected. He’s now expected to be out an extended period of time, and possibly for the rest of the season.
It’s very bad news for a team that showed great promise in Week 1, and it moves Jameis Winston into the starting job. He struggled in relief of Dart on Monday night, completing 11 of 27 passes for 111 yards and an interception.
The Giants have no other quarterbacks on the 53-man roster; Jake Haener is on the practice squad. Which means that the Giants will likely be scouring all available options for another player at the position — from free agency to a potential trade with a team that has a surplus at the position.
Originally, it was believed that Dart had an MCL sprain. Coach John Harbaugh told reporters on Monday night that the injury was in that “neighborhood.” Clearly, it wasn’t.

articles.title_orig: Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
articles.title_zh: Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
articles.content_orig:
Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
Britain’s newbie prime minister got through an hour with the U.S. president mostly unscathed. But the immediate differences were on show more than with Keir Starmer.
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump during a meeting on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026 in New York City. | Toby Melville/WPA Pool/Getty Images
NEW YORK — Before Andy Burnham’s meeting with Donald Trump, a senior U.K. government figure noted wryly that they were looking out for one thing — whether the U.S. president would claim that Burnham was better than the last guy.
After nearly an hour together in a cramped, low-ceilinged room in the United Nations basement, Trump did exactly that.
The president said U.K.-U.S. relations were “more up now than they were with your last prime minister.” Moments later he put the boot into Keir Starmer again, claiming the ex-PM’s tough rhetoric on Russia had been “too tough.”
That final comment will please Starmer, who welcomed Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Britain after Trump berated him in the Oval Office. But it also shows how far his relationship with Trump fell after his initial attempts to please the president in early 2025.
Burnham had the benefit of a fresh start, and ahead of his first meeting with Trump, British officials insisted he would take a less fawning approach than his predecessor. He could afford to do so, they said, because Trump’s presidency is almost at the midway point and there is less to lose.
Yet there were similarities to Starmer’s early days. Both leaders were on their best behavior, straining not to upset each other in public.
They each gave the other a free pass. Burnham sat expressionless as Trump talked about “fake news” media, while Trump did the same as Burnham talked about Britain’s recent sanctions on West Bank settlements.
Burnham raised the salience of immigration, an issue Trump invoked against Starmer, while Trump even praised Burnham’s “great election win.” (Burnham has not won a general election, merely a special election for the parliamentary seat of Makerfield.)
But some things were different. The splits between the two nations were closer to the surface than in Starmer’s first trip — and even in those cordial words for the cameras, the divides broke into the open.
Trump seized on a Daily Telegraph journalist’s invitation to condemn the long-stalled British plan to hand sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically vital archipelago in the Indian Ocean, to Mauritius. His words were little surprise on their own, but Burnham’s response — in which he repeatedly refused to rule out reopening the terms of the deal to satisfy Trump’s concerns — formed a genuine shift in U.K. policy.
It remains unclear how any deal could satisfy the demands of Mauritius and the U.S. at the same time.
Then there was the gulf between the two leaders on AI regulation.
Andy Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
Burnham used a breakfast Tuesday in New York with business figures, including Apple’s Tim Cook, to call for an agreed global set of standards on the technology.
Burnham spent almost an hour in a room with the leader of the free world (and an eight-strong delegation on each side), yet appears not to have raised AI with Trump at all. Downing Street repeatedly refused to say he brought it up and there was no mention of it the official readout.
After it was all over, Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage.
He also announced a “national center for information defense” (with little detail) that would counter disinformation; he portrayed Britain as an “honest broker” on controlling AI. But Britain’s decision not to back a declaration by 22 countries on global AI controls earlier in the week meant it could be sidelined. (Burnham said Britain would look at multiple initiatives, including that one.)
There were other potential wrinkles. Burnham said he would speak in defense of the Falkland Islands, weeks after Trump gave fuel to Argentina’s long-standing claims on their sovereignty by suggesting he would not help if Argentina tried to invade.
Burnham also revealed that he made a plea to Trump about U.S. tariffs and their effect on a particular factory in the northeast of England (he would not say which one). Despite the carve-outs that Starmer won, British industry — especially the automobile sector — is still being hit by Trump’s tariffs.
But so much that could have gone wrong, didn’t — at least for now. Trump did not use the time before the cameras to bring up Britain’s difficult progress toward spending 3.5% of GDP on defense, and did not hit out over the pace of the decision to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.
The newbie prime minister looked buttoned-up during the moment for the cameras with Trump, relaxing only when he was asked about Manchester, where he spent nine years as mayor. The world stage is still new to him.
And in that context, his aides will be chalking the first meeting up overall as a win — just as Starmer’s aides did on the way back from New York two years ago this week. Trump praised Burnham as a natural businessman, a man who “gets it.” The vibes, in this relatively easy opening period, were good.
He will need to maintain the influence if he can. Burnham later said he lobbied Trump to press for an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia. Pressure on the U.S. to release more air defense missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter will only increase.
While Burnham didn’t invite him to the U.K. on Tuesday, they did pave the way for another visit to one of Trump’s golf resorts. “I said I was having second thoughts about playing golf with him, given a recent performance of my own was probably not up to the right standard,” Burnham told broadcasters.
For the man who wasn’t going to bend the knee to Trump, flattery will get him everywhere.

articles.title_orig: Japan’s Leader Calls on U.N. to Drop ‘Enemy State’ Label
articles.title_zh: Japan’s Leader Calls on U.N. to Drop ‘Enemy State’ Label
articles.content_orig:
Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has voiced her country’s “consistent support” for the international criminal court (ICC), after Donald Trump urged member states to abandon the body, calling it “out of control”.
In her speech to the UN general assembly in New York on Tuesday, Takaichi said postwar Japan had “emphasised the rule of law in the resolution of all conflicts” – a commitment she said was reflected in its support for multilateral organisations such as the ICC.
Japan’s leader had faced pressure at home to publicly support the ICC, whose president, Tomoko Akane, is Japanese, after failing to come to its defence in response to Trump’s announcement in August that the US would impose sanctions targeting the entire organisation.
On Tuesday, Trump intensified his criticism of the ICC in his speech to the general assembly. “The United States is equally opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the international criminal court,” he said.
“I call on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.”
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has called for the ICC to be dismantled “brick by brick”, describing it as an “intolerable threat to US sovereignty”.
Takaichi avoided direct criticism of the US administration in her UN speech as she seeks to keep Washington on side amid rising tensions in the Asia-Pacific, including a commitment to support democratic Taiwan and address Chinese military activity in the South and East China Seas.
Officials in Tokyo are reportedly concerned that Trump could use Taiwan as leverage when he discusses trade with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington on Thursday.
Washington is legally obliged to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. Beijing regards the self-governing island as a province and has vowed to “annex” it, including by force if it can’t convince or coerce Taiwan into accepting what it calls “reunification”.
Takaichi’s most recent comments on the ICC come after a cross-party group of MPs in Japan urged her to demand that Trump withdraw the sanctions, announced in response to its decision to issue a warrant for the arrest of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and an ongoing investigation into alleged war crimes by American troops in Afghanistan.
One of the Japanese lawmakers, former defence minister Gen Nakatani, said the UN general assembly was “a place where a country should make its case to the world”, adding: “We want Japan to protect the ICC through the [prime minister’s] address and contacts with other countries.”
Takaichi said on Tuesday that she and Trump had a “candid exchange” about the ICC during discussions on the sidelines of the general assembly.
In the past, Takaichi had drawn criticism for her lukewarm defence of the ICC, having initially described US sanctions as “very unfortunate”. She later said the measures were “incompatible” with Japan’s stance on the work of the court.
Akane, who has led the ICC since 2024, said she would not be intimidated by the threat of sanctions. Speaking soon after the measures were announced in August, she told reporters: “The ICC will never be defeated. Justice will and should prevail, and we will stay true to that belief.”

articles.title_orig: New Adtech From Microsoft Would Interrupt Your Game at 'Promoted Content Trigger Events'
articles.title_zh: New Adtech From Microsoft Would Interrupt Your Game at 'Promoted Content Trigger Events'
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft already shows you ads whenever you log into the Xbox Series X, but it seems like it's exploring an ad-supported way to essentially rent out games on Xbox consoles.
Microsoft filed a patent called 'contextually aware management of interactive software application access,' which describes a process of pausing your game at the operating system level and presenting 'audiovisual promoted content' (in other words, an ad), which would then grant you a credit once it's over. That credit, at least in the way it's presented in the patent documentation, would grant you access to the game for a limited amount of time, from 15 minutes to an hour.
It's important to keep in mind that there's no way to tell whether or not the technology presented in this patent will ever get implemented. But, considering the troubles Xbox Game Pass has been dealing with lately, it's not that bizarre to imagine an ad-supported tier where you have to watch an ad every 15 minutes to keep playing your game.
Keep in mind that Microsoft also recently limited playtime on Xbox Cloud Gaming to just 15 hours a month with Game Pass Ultimate. That's not a lot of time to play games, and anyone relying on cloud streaming, now that RAM prices have gone through the roof, could be stuck dealing with the ads just to play games for more than 30 minutes a day.
Hopefully, if this patent does materialize into something real, it'll be a way to let people play for free, rather than being snuck into games that people paid full price for. However, even Disney+ looks like it's going to work ads into its most expensive subscription plan, so it's not off the table for Microsoft to do the same.
After all, this patent comes at a time when Microsoft is aggressively trying to make Xbox more profitable. The company just had another round of layoffs, where it handed Halo to Activision and got rid of a Halo Studios cinematic director the same week that he was promoted. Project Helix is also lurking around the corner, and it's probably going to be incredibly expensive, thanks to the ongoing RAM crisis.

articles.title_orig: Dancing With the Stars Eliminates 3rd Celebrity After "Shaky" Performance
articles.title_zh: Dancing With the Stars Eliminates 3rd Celebrity After "Shaky" Performance
articles.content_orig:
The dance floor just got a little less crowded.
Dancing With the Stars contestant Giada De Laurentiis was knocked out of the season 35 competition after ranking the lowest alongside ballroom pro Alan Bersten during week two.
In the Sept. 22 episode, the chef danced a tango to “Venus” by Shocking Blue, bringing the evening's "Viral Hits Night" theme to life.
But judge Bruno Tonioli called it a “salsa without spice” and told De Laurentiis she needed to “go for it” like “jumping off a cliff.” Meanwhile, judge Carrie Ann Inaba summed up the performance with one word: "Shaky."
After the judges revealed their scores of 12 out of 30, De Laurentiis noted, "It's disappointing, but hopefully people will vote for us, and I'll get another shot."
"I think I tend to go faster, and I need to learn to slow down," the 56-year-old explained. "That's my lesson to be learned."
After the elimination, she noted, "I tried my best, and it wasn't best enough, but I did try my best."
And the elimination marked the third star to lose their spot in line for the Mirrorball following the ABC hit's two-night premiere, beginning Sept. 15. Secret Lives of Mormon Wives' Conner Leavitt was the first celebrity sent home after a salsa with pro Adele Zaikman didn't bring enough heat to the judges' table opening night.
"Obviously, going home first was not how I wanted to end my Dancing With the Stars experience," Conner, husband of DWTS semi-finalist Whitney Leavitt, explained on TikTok Sept. 17. "But I can genuinely say I had an incredible time. I loved being out there. I loved learning something completely new."
Following his departure, Conner's fellow Hulu realityverse member Sarah Jane Nader was eliminated on night two. The Love Thy Nader personality was partnered with pro Hailey Bills, together becoming the show's third same-sex pairing. (JoJo Siwa and Jenna Johnson, who placed second on season 30, were the first.)
As such, the 24-year-old was proud of how her DWTS run honored her community as a bisexual woman, despite ending sooner than older sister Brooks Nader's ascent to ninth place with her now-ex Gleb Savchenko in 2024.
"As sad as we are to not dance next week—we were so excited—we're just grateful we had this opportunity," Sarah Jane told Good Morning America after the results. "Our partnership was so special. Not only because we became best friends, but because we represent a whole community."
But the 2026 competition is still anyone's game. Read on to see all of the stars still waltzing in for the win.

articles.title_orig: Second sea turtle spotted nesting on SoCal beach after historic sighting
articles.title_zh: Second sea turtle spotted nesting on SoCal beach after historic sighting
articles.content_orig:
2 different sea turtles nest on California beaches for the first time
Two sea turtles have laid eggs on Southern California beaches, marking the first recorded natural nesting of any sea turtle species on the West Coast.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) verified that two different turtles are nesting on Orange County beaches. Lifeguards spotted one of the turtles, an olive ridley sea turtle, last week on Surfside Beach. A second turtle was seen near Huntington Beach. Both areas have been roped off to protect the nests, which typically incubate for 45 to 60 days.
Experts say warmer waters caused by El Niño are driving the turtles north.
"There's extremely warm waters, much higher temperatures than would be normal for this time of year, and so it's created these quasi-tropical habitats right off the California coast," said Jeff Seminoff, the leader of the Marine Turtle Ecology and Assessment Program at the NOAA Southwest Fisheries Science Center.
While sea turtles have occasionally been spotted off California when the water gets warm, they have never nested on the West Coast. Typically, olive ridley sea turtles lay around 100 eggs on average and can have up to three nests.
The nesting event has been described as unprecedented.
"In my nearly 40 years of working with sea turtles, it's one of the most exciting and momentous occasions in my entire career," Seminoff said. "Never have I thought there would be sea turtles nesting here. It's an area where we have abundant green turtle populations living in our coastal waters, but to have turtles crawling onto our beaches is an entirely different situation."
This story was featured as part of our new California Tonight show. It airs Monday-Friday at 7:30 p.m. Watch on KCRA and KSBW.

articles.title_orig: El Niño goes wild: Pacific Ocean under siege from tropical cyclones
articles.title_zh: El Niño goes wild: Pacific Ocean under siege from tropical cyclones
articles.content_orig:
El Niño goes wild: Pacific Ocean under siege from tropical cyclones
The wild and woolly Pacific basin – fueled by a powerful El Niño – continues to spew forth tropical cyclones of all shapes and sizes. As of the afternoon of Sept. 22, a dangerous Category 5 180-mph hurricane (Hurricane Polo) was threatening the west coast of Mexico and pushing a swath of moisture into New Mexico.
At the same time, a smaller developing system was being watched nervously close to Hawaii.
And to top it off, yet another tropical cyclone, Odalys, could be drawn into a rare meteorological dance in the eastern Pacific with Polo known as the Fujiwhara Effect.
All the action in the Pacific is in contrast to the sleepy Atlantic basin, which has yet to see a single hurricane so far this year. Only six rather unremarkable tropical storms have formed there this season.
Polo explodes to Category 5
Hurricane Polo rapidly intensified into a Category 5 hurricane by the afternoon of Sept. 22 with peak sustained winds of 180 mph and higher gusts as it moves along just off the Mexican coast, according to the National Hurricane Center.
Overall, Polo's maximum sustained winds increased by an incredible 95 mph in 22 hours. (Between 3 p.m. on Sept. 21 and 1 p.m. on Sept. 22).
It's the third Category 5 hurricane in the eastern Pacific during this hurricane season, putting 2026 into a tie with the 1994 season as the most Category 5s on record by Sept. 22, Colorado State University hurricane scientist Phil Klotzbach posted on X.
Still, "despite its great strength, Polo remains a relatively small cyclone with its hurricane and tropical-storm-force winds estimated to only extend about 30 and 80 nautical miles from the eye, respectively," according to a Sept. 22 forecast discussion from the hurricane center.
Tropical Storm Odalys and the Fujiwhara effect
Otherwise unremarkable Tropical Storm (soon to be hurricane) Odalys could interact with Polo as the storms edge closer together off the coast of Mexico in a few days.
"A stunning scenario would be two major hurricanes side-by-side off the southern tip of Baja California, [while] one (Polo) or the other (Odalys) sling-shots away from the 'binary system,'" noted Weather Trader meteorologist Ryan Maue on X.
"Fujiwara Effect hurricane or typhoon interactions are highly unpredictable-->climate chaos!," Maue said on X.
The hurricane center mentions this interaction in their forecast discussion of Polo: "The steering currents become more uncertain over the weekend when Polo reaches the western edge of the ridge and nears Tropical Storm Odalys to its west."
And it's also mentioned in the Odalys (pronounced oh-DAL-ess) discussion: "After day three, the uncertainty in the track increases due to potential interaction with Hurricane Polo, which could cause Odalys to slow down late in the forecast period."
What is the Fujiwhara effect?
When two storms or hurricanes spinning in the same direction pass close enough to each other, they begin an intense dance around their common center known as the Fujiwhara effect, the National Weather Service said.
The effect is thought to occur when storms get about 900 miles apart.
Storms involved in the Fujiwhara effect are rotating around one another as if they had locked arms and were square dancing. Rather than each storm spinning about the other, they are actually moving about a central point between them, as if both were tied to the same post and each swung around it separately of the other.
A good way to picture this is to think of two ice skaters who skate quickly toward each other, nearly on a collision course, grab hands as they are about to pass and spin vigorously around in one big circle with their joined hands at the center.
According to Weather.com, the stronger storm often dominates, tugging the weaker one into its circulation, but in rare cases, two storms of similar strength can combine, creating a single, more powerful storm.
Hawaii in the crosshairs again
Hawaiian Island residents, who have felt the influence of six tropical storms or hurricanes already this year, are being asked to watch the weather closely yet again as a seventh potential storm could bring rain to the Big Island as early as Sept. 23.
The potential storm is actually the remnants of Tropical Depression Fifteen-E, which dissipated on Sept. 15. The hurricane center indicates environmental conditions are favorable for the remnants to become a tropical depression again, with the chances of storm formation at 70% over 48 hours and 90% over the next seven days.
By Sept. 24, computer forecast models show a potential tropical cyclone drifting toward the Big Island, according to the weather service office in Honolulu. Heavy rains associated with the storm are forecast to spread over the southeastern Hawaiian Islands starting Sept. 23, whether or not it organizes into a named storm, the national weather service said.
While the strength and position of the storm still appear highly uncertain, there’s "a significant potential for a prolonged heavy rain event" over the windward and southeast areas of the Big Island, the weather service warned. A flood watch could be issued later in the week.
Potential wind impacts also remain uncertain, but the weather service indicates a "high likelihood" of at least gusty trade winds of 50 to 60 mph by Sept. 25.
Polo to push rain into New Mexico
As Hurricane Polo moves along in the Pacific south of Mexico, it's helping to push an intense swath of tropical moisture northward into New Mexico this week, said Bob Oravec, a meteorologist at the weather service's Weather Prediction Center.
"Even though Polo will remain well offshore, some of its higher moisture values are being drawn northward," Oravec said. In general the Albuquerque weather service region is forecast to receive an average of 3 to 4 inches of rain through Friday, with the potential for more than 5 inches in some isolated locations.
Doyle Rice and Dinah Voyles Pulver are national correspondents for USA TODAY with a focus on weather and climate. Reach them at drice@usatoay.com and dpulver@usatoday.com.

articles.title_orig: At U.N., Carney Lays Out a Broad Plan for a Divided World
articles.title_zh: At U.N., Carney Lays Out a Broad Plan for a Divided World
articles.content_orig: UNITED NATIONS — Canada’s Representative to the United Nations made the case for multilateralism after Prime Minister Mark Carney missed the event at the General Assembly on Monday because of technical problems at a key regional air traffic control centre that halted operations at every major airport in the New York City area. Hundreds of flights were cancelled in the U.S. northeast after a key circuit failed at an air traffic facility in Philadelphia. The Prime Minister’s Office said Carney arrived in New York City later Monday night. Canada’s Ambassador to the United Nations David Lametti spoke in Carney’s place during a roundtable discussion on strengthening multilateral collaboration with European Council President António Costa and Kenya’s President William Ruto on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The discussion took place at the Partners for Multilateralism summit, or P4M, a gathering of leaders to discuss coalition-building and translating shared principles into practical action. Lametti said Carney has spoke about the “rupture” the world is living through — referencing the prime minister’s widely applauded speech in Davos earlier this year — but now it is time to talk about what’s next. He said coalitions of the willing must come together to deal with specific issues and find ways to actionable results. Lametti said nations ready to act should “build trust and prove what works” and then bring it back to the larger multilateralism structure. Carney, Costa, Ruto and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva co-wrote an opinion piece published Sunday in The Financial Times that argues the global community is more interdependent than ever, “even as it becomes more fragmented and polarized.” They pointed to climate change, global pandemics, financial shocks, conflicts and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as global crises that require countries to work together. “Cooperation is therefore not an act of idealism, it is a practical necessity,” the leaders wrote. “The question is not whether multilateralism can survive, but how it must evolve to meet the realities of our time.” Trump’s return to the White House and his unpredictable tariff campaign have upended global institutions and pushed away traditional allies. Trump and members of his administration have demanded significant changes to the UN and have held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil. Brazil’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Mauro Vieira didn’t mention Trump by name but said there are nations who want to make the world into spheres of influence, language used by the current U.S. administration. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese talked about middle power countries that need to come together, “stepping up and being outward looking.” As Trump looks to realign the global order, Carney has emerged in the role of coalition builder — something that appears to irritate the president. Earlier Monday, Trump posted on social media that the United States is working on a “massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus.” “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers,” Trump said. Details of that proposed deal remain unclear. It’s the latest shot Trump has taken at Canada since trade talks broke down in acrimony last month. On Bloomberg Television on Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer again accused Canada of ending the trade talks and claimed the escalating tariff war won’t have much of an impact on the U.S. economy. Greer said Canada now wants to “get together” with the European Union. That’s a reference to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen using her state of the union address to the European Parliament last week to open the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member.” “They’ve been very clear over the past year and a half, they’re sovereign. They may want to tie up with the EU now so it raises the question of that whole sovereignty shtick,” Greer said. Trump is set to give a speech in front of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is set to deliver a speech to the General Assembly later in the week. Carney, who is scheduled to be in New York City from Monday to Wednesday, is still expected to attend a discussion on the two-state solution in the Middle East on Tuesday and meet with global and business leaders on the sidelines of the event. For nearly a year now, Carney has been promoting the idea of bringing countries around the world together to pursue what he has called “shared interests, and occasionally shared values, rather than shared institutions.” Carney has sought to build a bridge between the EU and a Pacific Rim trading bloc called CPTPP so that middle powers can better resist economic coercion by the U.S. and China. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026. - With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

articles.title_orig: Ex-Canadian soldier opens fire at synagogue on Yom Kippur, wounds cop in possible antisemitic attack: officials
articles.title_zh: Ex-Canadian soldier opens fire at synagogue on Yom Kippur, wounds cop in possible antisemitic attack: officials
articles.content_orig:
Ex-Canadian soldier opens fire at synagogue on Yom Kippur, wounds cop in possible antisemitic attack: officials
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
An ex-Canadian soldier opened fire outside a synagogue during Yom Kippur services and struck a cop before being gunned down by police in a possible antisemitic attack, officials said.
Shotgun-toting Sean Ward, 29, pulled up in his truck and ripped off shots at two cops stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, around 7 p.m. Sunday, according to the CBC.
Ward struck Constable Jeff Smith, who was working security outside the synagogue along with another cop. The two officers returned fire and hit Ward, who died of his injuries Monday night.
Smith remained in critical but stable condition as of Tuesday.
It was not immediately clear if Ward was targeting the synagogue — located about 110 miles east of Toronto — or law enforcement.
Investigators, however, noted that the timing of the shooting on Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, suggests the attack may have been motivated by antisemitism.
None of the roughly two dozen congregants inside were injured, but bullets peppered surrounding homes, vehicles and the synagogue’s windows.
“There are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me and some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot out windows, that sort of thing. So it would have been quite the scene,” Belleville Deputy Police Chief Sheri Meeks said.
Worshipers said they immediately realized gunfire was erupting outside and ducked for cover during the intense exchange of about 25 shots, which lasted mere moments.
“I could say, ‘Oh, this is definitely … someone is shooting here,'” Norm Weddum, the leader of Sons of Jacob, who was in attendance for the service, told CBC. “So that’s when we ran back into the auditorium of the synagogue, closed the doors behind us so as to not leave a visible target and we hit the floor.
“Literally everyone went down. I yelled for everyone to get on to the floor and the shots continued for a few more seconds, and then it was basically over.”
Sons of Jacob always requests extra security on Jewish High Holidays due to threat concerns, Weddum noted.
“Thank God that person was there,” he said, referring to Smith.
Authorities are probing a motive in the shooting.
“It’s believed that [Ward] came in a truck and he had a shotgun and he discharged his firearm at a police officer and then that police officer returned fire and then there was a second officer who arrived and then also discharged [their] firearm,” Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit, told reporters.
Ward joined the Canadian Armed Forces in 2017 and served as an infantry soldier before leaving in 2022 as a corporal.
Meeks said antisemitism has “no place” in Belleville — and announced a heightened police presence across the city.
“Let me be very clear: Antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community,” she said.
“Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones, or participating in community life.”
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis all condemned the attack.

articles.summary_zh: 一名联邦法官已定于周四就州检察长与派拉蒙华纳兄弟探索公司之间的拟议和解举行听证会。美国地区法官Araceli Martinez Olguin通过Zoom将听证会定在太平洋时间上午11点。她在周二的一份命令中写道，听证会将“解决有关各方拟议同意令的事实和法律基础以及拟议同意令执行情况的某些悬而未决的问题”
articles.content_orig:
A federal judge has set a hearing for Thursday on the proposed settlement between state attorneys general and Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery.
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin set the hearing for 11 a.m. PT via Zoom.
She wrote in an order Tuesday that the hearing would be to “address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and legal underpinnings of the parties proposed consent decree, as well as the implementation of the proposed consent decree.”
The parties have filed a motion to approve the consent decree, which lays out a series of settlement conditions to resolve the lawsuit brought by the state AGs in July. Among the provisions are Paramount commitments to release at least 30 movies per year, and another to create an independent board to oversee CNN and CBS News adherence to journalistic standards.
The judge also canceled a scheduled hearing on whether to require the state AGs to post a bond as the litigation proceeded.
The judge said in a separate order that she would decide in “due course” on whether to dismiss the lawsuit brought by the Writers Guild of America to block the merger. The WGA said it also reached a settlement with Paramount to end its litigation.
